## Guides
- Spring Wire Gauge (SWG) Chart — SWG to mm & inch: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/spring-wire-gauge-swg-chart.html — SWG (Standard Wire Gauge) is a wire-size scale where a higher number means thinner wire — for example SWG 14 is 2.032 mm (0.080 in) and SWG 20 is 0.914 mm (0.036 in).
- Compression Spring Rate Formula (with worked example): https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/spring-rate-formula-compression-spring.html — Compression spring rate is k = G·d⁴ / (8·D³·Na), where G is the shear modulus, d the wire diameter, D the mean coil diameter and Na the number of active coils.
- How to Measure a Spring for Replacement or a Quote: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/how-to-measure-a-spring.html — To measure a spring, record wire diameter, outer diameter, free length, number of coils, end type, winding direction and material — with these a manufacturer can quote or reproduce it.
- Mild Steel vs Stainless Steel vs Music Wire Springs — Which to Choose?: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/mild-steel-vs-stainless-steel-vs-music-wire-springs.html — Choose stainless steel when corrosion resistance matters, music wire for high strength and fatigue life in dry conditions, and mild (carbon) steel for the lowest cost in general machinery — usually with a protective coating.
- Custom Spring Cost: What Affects the Price and What to Send for a Quote: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/custom-spring-cost-and-quote-checklist.html — Custom spring price depends mainly on wire material and size, spring type and complexity, quantity, tolerances and testing, and finishing — send full specifications to get an accurate quote.
- Extension Spring Load & Rate Formula (with worked example): https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/extension-spring-load-formula.html — Extension spring load is F = F0 + k·x, where F0 is initial tension, k the spring rate (same formula as a compression spring) and x the extension beyond free length.
- Torsion Spring Torque & Rate Formula (with worked example): https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/torsion-spring-torque-formula.html — Torsion spring rate is k = E·d⁴ / (64·D·N) in N·mm per radian, where E is the modulus of elasticity, d wire diameter, D mean coil diameter and N active coils; torque = k × angle.
- Spring End Types Explained — Closed, Ground and Open Ends: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/spring-end-types-explained.html — Compression springs commonly have open, closed, or closed-and-ground ends; closed and ground ends sit flat and square for the best stability, and closed ends typically add two inactive coils (total coils = active coils + 2).
- Spring Finishes & Coatings — Zinc, Black Oxide, Powder Coat, Passivation: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/spring-finishes-and-coatings.html — Zinc plating and powder coating protect carbon steel springs from rust, black oxide gives light protection, and stainless steel springs are passivated; high-strength plated springs may need baking to reduce hydrogen embrittlement risk.
- IS 4454 Spring Wire Standard Explained: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/is-4454-spring-wire-grades-explained.html — IS 4454 is the Indian Standard for spring steel wire, split into parts by process: Part 1 covers cold-drawn unalloyed wire (grades by static or dynamic duty), Part 2 covers oil-hardened and tempered wire, and Part 4 (now IS 4454:2018) covers stainless steel spring wire for corrosion resistance.
- Die Spring Colour Code Chart — Light, Medium, Heavy & Extra-Heavy: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/die-spring-colour-code-chart.html — Die springs are colour-coded by duty (load) level — commonly light, medium, heavy and extra-heavy — but the exact colour used for each duty level is not identical across every standard or manufacturer, so always confirm against the specific catalogue rather than colour alone.
- Trampoline Spring Buying Guide — Size, Count & Replacement Tips: https://industrialspringmanufacturer.com/guides/trampoline-spring-buying-guide.html — To replace trampoline springs, measure the free length of an existing spring end-to-end (including hooks), count how many springs your trampoline uses, and match both the length and the hook style — most residential trampolines use springs roughly 140–230 mm long.
